title: Count the stars (Genesis 15:1–6)
hookLine: childless and old, Abram is taken outside: count the stars

cards: Some promises get harder to believe the longer you wait. The job that was coming. The test results that would be fine.
The baby that would come someday. Abram has been promised a great nation, children like the dust of the earth. Years have gone by.
He's won a war, rescued Lot, been blessed by a king. But his tent is still quiet. No son, no daughter.
And one night, God speaks to him again in a vision, and this time Abram talks back. Not with a song of praise. With the thing that's been keeping him up at night.

teach.b: God opens with comfort, in the King James Bible: "Fear not, Abram: I am thy shield, and thy exceeding great reward."
And Abram answers, honestly: what will you give me, seeing I go childless? My heir is a servant born in my house. It's not polite.
It's real. And God doesn't scold him. Instead God does something simple.
God brings him outside. An old man stepping out of his tent into a desert night, with no city lights anywhere, the whole sky crowded.
"Look now toward heaven, and tell the stars, if thou be able to number them: and he said unto him, So shall thy seed be." Tell the stars means count them. He can't, of course.
Nobody could. Then comes the sentence the rest of the chapter turns on: "And he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness." Believed.
In Hebrew, he'emin, from the root aman, to be firm, to hold steady. It's the root of the very first word on this hill: amen.
Abram said amen to the stars.
He leaned his weight on a promise he still couldn't see. Remember Romans, a few weeks ago? Paul quotes this verse in chapter four: Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness.
He quotes it again in Galatians, and the letter of James quotes it too. It starts with an old man outside his tent, trying to count.

how: Genesis 15:6 is central to Christian teaching on faith: Paul quotes it in Romans 4 and Galatians 3, and James 2 quotes it too, and it is often preached on when churches talk about faith.

o: a Greek word that marks the end of a prayer
a Latin word that means praise be to God
from a root meaning to be firm, to hold steady

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: God's first words in the vision
he believed, from the root of amen

s: Abram answers God's promise with a song of praise
he answers honestly: what will you give me, seeing I go childless?
the Hebrew word for believed shares a root with amen
he'emin, from aman: to be firm, to lean your weight on.
Paul quotes this verse in his letter to the Romans
"Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness."

games.q: you're old and childless, and God has just promised you a great reward. what do you say?
o: "what will you give me, seeing I go childless?"
games.why: Abram says the thing keeping him up at night. God doesn't scold him. God takes him outside to count the stars.

practice: If it's dark where you are, look up at the night sky, or picture the clearest one you've seen, and try to count: notice how fast you give up, and how more appear the longer you look.
Then hold a promise you're still waiting on under those stars, without forcing it. If you pray, you can say amen to it.

wordCard.voice: Amen. The Hebrew root for believed, to be firm: what Abram said to a promise he couldn't see, so shall thy seed be.

orig.note: Hebrew: he believed, from the root aman, to be firm, the same root as amen.

carryVoice: Your line: so shall your seed be. He couldn't count them, and he believed. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: Fear not, Abram: I am thy shield, and thy exceeding great reward.
Look now toward heaven, and tell the stars, if thou be able to number them: and he said unto him, So shall thy seed be.
And he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness.
Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness.
